implementation_notes: The JavaScript idiom is a shallow copy literal: `{ ...person, home: { ...person.home, city: 'Berlin' } }` replaces the hand-written copy cascade for one level and nests for depth, while `structuredClone` (Node 17+, modern browsers) produces a full deep clone when sharing is not wanted. Object spread is the mechanism lens libraries are built on, so it needs no dependency and stays the right choice for a single fixed path; hand-roll a focus only when the same path must be stored, passed or reused across modules.
pitfalls: The spread is shallow at every level you do not spell out: nested objects and arrays are shared, so a later in-place mutation of the "old" value is visible in the new one.
Spreading a class instance copies own enumerable properties only - the prototype (and therefore methods) is dropped, and getters are evaluated into plain values.
Non-enumerable and symbol-keyed state is silently lost in the copy, which breaks objects that keep state in closures or non-enumerable properties.

variants.name: Ramda lens functions (R.lens/R.lensPath + view/set/over)
variants.idiom_name: Ramda R.lens / R.lensPath with R.view / R.set / R.over
variants.implementation_notes: Ramda is the mainstream JavaScript library that actually implements lenses: `R.lensPath(['home', 'city'])` (or `R.lensProp`/`R.lens` for one level) creates the optic, and `R.view`, `R.set` and `R.over` apply it, so a path becomes a value that can be stored, passed and reused - the composition that the spread literal cannot express. Ramda's setters clone along the path immutably and copy by reference elsewhere, which keeps the pattern's copy discipline; reach for it when paths are data or derived from configuration, and keep the spread literal for a one-off update.
pitfalls: Ramda functions are curried: forgetting the final value returns a function instead of a result, so a typo turns into a silent no-op that only fails at the next use.
R.set/R.over clone along the path but copy everything else by reference, so non-path nested objects are still shared with the original.
Lenses over arrays use index paths, which shift when the array changes: a stored `lensPath(['items', 0])` silently retargets another element after an unshift.
